items.central_claim_check: Confirmed. (a) The lane is one build for two projects: web/playwright.e2e.config.ts:24-53 (projects `e2e` for *.e2e.ts and `chromium` for *.vr.ts) over one webServer whose env is inlined at build time (lines 55-68). With the spec's fake ID and Sydney for every project, every page of every case starts Google Analytics. (b) Four files import `test` straight from @playwright/test and never install a Google fixture: web/e2e/player.e2e.ts:3, web/e2e/a11y.e2e.ts:2, web/e2e/pages.vr.ts:3 and web/e2e/toast-occlusion.e2e.ts:14. They hold 98 cases today (76 + 9 + 10 + 3; the last file loops over three widths at line 37). None is named in section 1's changed files. (c) failOnUnexpectedPageErrors() (web/e2e/page-errors.ts:90-123) listens to 'pageerror' only (line 97): not console errors, not failed requests. player.e2e.ts:10, a11y.e2e.ts:16 and pages.vr.ts:65 call it; toast-occlusion.e2e.ts does not. The lane's only console listener (player.e2e.ts:25) filters for AlphaTab lines. No lane test installs a catch-all route (all routes in player-states.ts and player.e2e.ts target the app's own paths). (d) The Sentry spec (PR #191), section 6: every build gets the fake DSN https://public@sentry.invalid/1 and 'One shared fixture routes every request to that host'; a case without that fixture is harmless only because a .invalid host never resolves (this review's spike: an unrouted POST to sentry.invalid is rejected). Google's hosts do resolve. (e) The 2026-10-05 spike (throwaway, not in the repo) routed only Google's collect hosts, so its gtag.js came live from Google: line 451's 'so nothing reached Google' is not exact. (f) A made-up ID gets a working script: about 440 KB, served with cache-control 'private, max-age=900', and it sends a page view (spike case 2). (g) Google Analytics terms, sections 1 and 4 (https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/): the 'Software' includes the GAMC (the Google Analytics Measurement Code, which is gtag.js), and section 4 forbids copying it, changing it or making derivative works of it. (h) The `web` job runs in a Playwright container pinned by sha256 digest (.github/workflows/ci.yml:436-458) and blocks merge (AGENTS.md, 'VR & a11y testing'); CI retries a failing case twice (playwright.e2e.config.ts:18).

spike.what: A local page that runs section 4's startAnalytics() sketch as written (a made-up ID, the spec's consent default, `config` with Google signals and ad personalisation off and `release`, the script added after `load`), driven by the installed Playwright 1.61.1 and its Chromium 149 as Sydney. Chromium started with --host-resolver-rules making www.googletagmanager.com and *.google-analytics.com unresolvable (and once with a wider set adding analytics.google.com, www.google.com and *.doubleclick.net). Case 1: no route. Case 2: a context route that downloads gtag.js with route.fetch() and answers every other Google request locally with 204. Case 3: a route that answers gtag.js with an empty script. Then four script-loader shapes under the rule, to see which raise a Playwright page error. Nothing left the machine but downloads of gtag.js (case 2, and two direct downloads to read its header); no hit was sent.
spike.result: Case 1: the script request fails (net::ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED); no page error; one console error ('Failed to load resource'); no hit; no cookie. Case 2: route.fetch() returns the real script (status 200, 440,795 bytes) although the browser cannot resolve the host; requests to the unresolvable hosts are still routed and recorded. The page view arrives about 0.9 s after the page starts loading, with gcs=G101, npa=1, dt=Notation Hero and ep.release. Two custom events sent together arrive in one batched request 5,010 ms later (5,006 ms on the rerun with the wide rules). Leaving the page sends user_engagement to both www.google-analytics.com and www.google.com/g/collect. Cookies _ga and _ga_<ID> are set. Case 3: no request besides the script, no cookie; window.dataLayer holds exactly the consent default, js, config and the two events. Loader shapes: appending the script, or an onerror that reports and returns, raise no page error; an uncaught promise rejection or a throwing onerror each raise one, which would fail every case in the three gated files.

items.scenario: You push a one-line fix to the player. While the merge check runs, its test browser opens Notation Hero's pages about a hundred times, each time as a visitor in Sydney. Each time, Google's tracking script downloads from Google and sends a page view under the tests' made-up ID — from a test, to Google. The spec says no test reaches Google. Nearly every test does.
items.whats_wrong: Section 9 says the new fixture keeps every test away from Google, but only privacy-choice.e2e.ts uses it. The lane's one build gets the fake ID and every project runs as Sydney, so Google Analytics starts on every page of the 98 existing cases, in four files that never install the fixture. Sentry's fake address can never resolve; Google's addresses do, so those pages download Google's script and send real hits. Also, the spec never says where the fixture gets Google's script: the gcs, npa and dt checks need the real one, while 'answers Google's hosts locally' rules it out. A copy kept in the repository is not possible: Google Analytics' terms forbid copying its measurement code.

items.recommendation: 'No Google script in tests'. The `web` job blocks every merge and pins even its container by digest. A live script, which Google can change at any time (its cache lifetime is 15 minutes), would let Google's uptime and Google's own changes fail pull requests that cannot fix them. The privacy promise is about what our code hands Google, and this option checks all of it, at once, with no 5-second waits. Google's encoding has been seen twice (the 2026-10-05 spike and this review's spike: gcs=G101, npa=1, dt=Notation Hero), and section 8 step 6 checks it again on the real property, which no test with a made-up ID can show.
items.flip_condition: Choose 'Live script, hits kept local' if you want CI to notice by itself when Google changes how its script encodes consent or the title, and you accept that the privacy cases fail when www.googletagmanager.com is slow or unavailable (CI retries each failure twice).
items.proposed_fix: Close the leak in the config, for every case at once: Chromium's --host-resolver-rules launch argument makes Google's hosts unresolvable inside the test browser, so a case without the fixture cannot reach Google and fails nothing. Then decide where the fixture's gtag.js comes from: the live script through route.fetch(), with every other request answered locally, or an empty script, with the checks moved to what our code queues and Google's output checked by hand at launch.
items.why_it_works: The resolver rule is the same idea as Sentry's .invalid address: inside the test browser the hosts cannot be found, so a case that forgets the fixture sends nothing, and a new test file is covered without any edit. Playwright's routes act before the address lookup, so the fixture still sees and answers every request (spike case 2). route.fetch() runs in Node, not in the browser, so the live script still arrives when that option is chosen.

quotes.quote: "Report errors only": a forced error reaches Sentry, and nothing reaches Google.
With "Report errors only", Sentry starts without its Release Health session integration, so no visit ping is sent.
Sentry 11 can start after the page has loaded, and the name of its Release Health integration.

items.central_claim_check: Confirmed. The Sentry spec (PR #191), section 6: its fixture 'routes every request to that host, answers it, and records the envelope', and its cases 'read event envelopes only, never the session envelope that Release Health (S4) sends on every visit'. So the fixture can see session envelopes; NH-124's cases ignore them on purpose, and no case checks that one is absent. Sentry's docs list browserSessionIntegration as enabled by default for Next.js, and a default integration is removed by its name (https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/nextjs/configuration/integrations/). The SDK source names it 'BrowserSession' (https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/blob/develop/packages/browser/src/integrations/browsersession.ts). The Sentry spec's own filter removes default integrations by name (its section 3.3), so a wrong or renamed name leaves the visit ping on with no error. In the SDK core, an error captured during an active session sends a session update before the error itself (packages/core/src/client.ts, _updateSessionFromEvent and _processEvent), and the item type is 'session' (packages/core/src/envelope.ts). Sentry SDK major version 11 exists (the BrowserSession docs page notes a default that changed in version 11). The spec's 'To verify at plan time' still lists the integration's name (line 441).
items.contradicts: none — checked section 2's table (lines 101-107: 'Report errors only' sends error reports and no visit count), section 6 (lines 296-297), 'To verify at plan time' (line 441), and the Sentry spec's section 6 (its own cases ignore session envelopes; these cases would read them, which its fixture allows).

spike.what: From a local page, two POSTs to https://sentry.invalid/api/1/envelope/ (the shape Sentry's fake DSN produces), one carrying an item of type event and one of type session, through a Playwright 1.61.1 route that records each body; then the same POST with the route removed.
spike.result: Both were routed before any address lookup and recorded, and the item type was readable from the body; with no route, the POST was rejected ('Failed to fetch'). Sentry itself was not run (untested): @sentry/nextjs is not installed on this branch and installs are not allowed here, so its session behaviour comes from the SDK source.

items.scenario: You open Notation Hero in Berlin and press 'Report errors only'. You expect Sentry to hear from you only when something breaks. Months later, a Sentry upgrade renames the part that counts visits, the filter no longer removes it, and every page you open sends a visit ping. No test notices: the Berlin test checks only that an error arrives.
items.whats_wrong: Section 6 promises that 'Report errors only' starts Sentry without its visit-counting part, so no visit ping is sent. The Berlin test for that answer checks only that a forced error reaches Sentry and that nothing reaches Google. The part's name is still unverified (the spec's own 'To verify at plan time' list), and Sentry removes parts by name, so a wrong or renamed name keeps the ping on without any error.

The forced error is a fair moment to check: if the visit-counting part were still running, Sentry would send a session update before the error itself. The 'Yes' check proves the recorder can see session envelopes at all, so an empty result means something.
